weaknesses: The technical novelty is limited. SV is essentially a multi-model rationale ensemble followed by a stronger judge model; the connection to speculative decoding is analogical, with no token acceptance, distribution preservation, or demonstrated speculative-inference acceleration. Comparisons to self-consistency, rationale aggregation, and judge-based ensemble methods are discussed but not evaluated adequately.

The proposed consensus-score derivation has a serious conceptual issue. Writing L_j(y)=NLL_j(y), the score satisfies s(y_i)=sum_{j≠i}[L_j(y_i)-L_j(y_j)]=sum_j L_j(y_i)-sum_j L_j(y_j). The second term is constant across candidates, so the claimed normalization against each peer's own answer does not calibrate the ranking at all; it is equivalent to ranking by summed raw NLL. Such NLLs are not directly comparable across heterogeneous tokenizers and calibrations and can favor short or linguistically generic answers. No analysis addresses this issue.

The central cost-efficiency claim is unsupported. Reported cost includes only the GPT-4o verdict call, omitting five initial draft decodes, cross-model answer scoring, three additional rationale generations, PP-StructureV3 preprocessing, and local inference hardware costs. There is no end-to-end latency, FLOP, token, memory, or monetary comparison against GPT-4o alone or alternative ensembles. Moreover, the verdict consumes multiple long rationales and, on most datasets, two images.

Evaluation does not cleanly attribute gains to the proposed selection mechanism. Important baselines such as random or fixed top-three selection, semantic majority/self-consistency, and comparable rationale-aggregation judges are missing. Using all five experts is as good as or better than three on two benchmarks, while the best-reference strategy substantially exceeds cross-all on ChartMuseum. The strongest conclusion supported is therefore that supplying multiple rationales to a large model helps, not that the proposed consensus method is particularly effective.

The comparison involving PP-StructureV3 appears confounded: the structured image is supplied to the SV verdict, but an otherwise identical GPT-4o-plus-structured-image baseline is not reported. This input contributes 4.6 points on ChartQAPro, a material fraction of the claimed gain over GPT-4o.

No confidence intervals, repeated-run variability, or statistical tests are provided, despite stochastic proprietary inference and some gains being only about 1–2 points. It is also unclear whether choices such as m=3 were selected using a held-out validation set rather than the reported test sets.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The abstract's “Code is available at” field is blank and the PDF contains no repository link despite claiming that code is released. The ChartQAPro prompt remains a placeholder, the initial candidate-answer prompt is absent, and decoding parameters, model revisions, image-resolution settings, answer normalization, and evaluation details are insufficiently specified.

There are notable reporting inconsistencies: Table 4 appears to swap the numbers of images and questions for every dataset, and Table 3's caption mentions a 1,000-sample InfographicVQA subset while also reporting other benchmarks. These errors further obscure the exact evaluation sample sizes and protocol.
